texts.historicalContext: Monet painted the outer harbour of Le Havre from a hotel window in the early morning. Exhibited in 1874, the picture prompted Louis Leroy’s mocking label ‘Impressionists’, which the artists soon adopted.
texts.artisticAnalysis: Dark boats guide the eye toward cranes, masts and chimneys dissolving into blue-grey mist. The slightly off-centre orange sun and its vertical broken reflection organise the scene against the horizontal strokes of the water.
texts.palette: Thin, rapid, visible strokes preserve changing light rather than describing every object. Orange and blue-grey act as complementary colours, making the sun appear unusually intense; viewed from farther away, the eye assembles the separate marks into a convincing harbour.
texts.culturalSignificance: The modestly sized painting became a defining statement of modern vision: immediate perception replaces polished academic description, while natural light shares the scene with the industry and movement of a modern port.
interestingFacts: It depicts the port of Le Havre at dawn.
Its title inspired the name Impressionism after the 1874 exhibition.
